companion.title: Two coin tosses and a stubborn misconception
companion.subtitle: Independence, the gambler's fallacy, and counting ordered outcomes for a fair coin

chapters.title: Fair coins have no memory
chapters.goal: Understand independence and why past tosses do not make an outcome 'due'.

claims.text: For an ideal fair coin, heads and tails each have probability one half on any single toss.
claims.reason: cue-1 states heads and tails each have probability one half on a toss for an ideal fair coin.

claims.text: Independence means knowing one toss's result does not change the probability distribution for the next toss.
claims.reason: cue-1 gives exactly this definition of independence.

claims.text: Saying tails is 'due' after three heads in a row is a mistake for an independent fair coin; the next toss still has a one-half chance of tails.
claims.reason: cue-2 quotes the student's 'due' claim, calls it a mistake, and states tails remains one half.

claims.text: The coin has no memory of earlier outcomes.
claims.reason: cue-2 states the coin has no memory of earlier outcomes.

checks.question: A fair coin, tossed independently, lands heads three times in a row. What is the probability of tails on the next toss?

choices.text: Greater than one half, because tails is due.
choices.explanation: This is the misconception the source rejects: the coin has no memory, so earlier heads do not raise the chance of tails.
Correct. Independence means earlier results do not change the next toss's distribution; tails remains one half.

choices.text: Less than one half, because the coin is 'on a heads streak'.
choices.explanation: Also a memory-based error; the source's fair independent model assigns one half regardless of prior streaks.

recovery.question: What does independence of tosses mean, according to the source?

choices.text: Knowing one toss's result does not change the probabilities for the next toss.
Heads and tails must alternate over time.
Each toss cancels out the previous toss.

recovery.explanation: cue-1 defines independence as knowing one result not changing the next toss's probability distribution.

chapters.title: Counting ordered outcomes
chapters.goal: Compute probabilities for two tosses by listing the four ordered outcomes.

claims.text: Two independent fair tosses have four ordered outcomes—HH, HT, TH, TT—each with probability one quarter.
claims.reason: cue-3 lists the four ordered outcomes and assigns each probability one quarter.

claims.text: Order matters when listing the elementary outcomes.
claims.reason: cue-3 states order matters when listing elementary outcomes.

claims.text: Exactly one head has probability one half because HT and TH are two distinct outcomes; counting only one would miss half the favorable cases.
claims.reason: cue-4 gives HT and TH as distinct, probability one half, and warns that counting one misses half the favorable outcomes.

claims.text: Two heads has probability one quarter, and at least one head has probability three quarters.
claims.reason: cue-4 gives two heads as one quarter; cue-5 gives at least one head as three quarters.

claims.text: At least one head can also be found by subtracting the probability of no heads (TT) from one.
claims.reason: cue-5 describes subtracting the probability of no heads (tails-tails) from one.

checks.concept: Probability of exactly one head in two tosses
checks.question: In two independent fair tosses, what is the probability of exactly one head?

choices.explanation: This counts only one of HT or TH, missing half the favorable outcomes, as the source warns.
Correct. HT and TH are two distinct outcomes of four, giving one half.
That is the probability of at least one head, which also includes HH.

recovery.question: Which outcomes make up the event 'at least one head' in two tosses, and what is its probability?

choices.text: HT and TH only; one half

recovery.explanation: cue-5 lists HH, HT, TH for at least one head, probability three quarters; equivalently one minus P(TT).

chapters.title: What a model does and does not promise
chapters.goal: Distinguish model assumptions from guarantees about small samples.

claims.text: A probability model describes assumptions, not a guarantee that every small batch matches expected proportions.
claims.reason: cue-6 states a model describes assumptions, not a guarantee for small batches.

claims.text: Four tosses need not contain exactly two heads.
claims.reason: cue-6 states four tosses do not have to contain exactly two heads.

claims.text: If the coin is biased or tosses are dependent, the fair independent model must be reconsidered.
claims.reason: cue-6 states the model must be reconsidered if the coin is biased or tosses are dependent.

checks.question: A fair coin is tossed four times. What does the model say about the number of heads?

choices.explanation: The source says a model gives assumptions, not guarantees; four tosses need not have exactly two heads.

choices.text: It does not guarantee exactly two heads; small batches can deviate from expected proportions.
choices.explanation: Correct, matching the source's statement about models and small batches.

choices.text: Any deviation from two heads proves the coin is biased.
choices.explanation: The source says deviation in a small batch is possible under the fair model; bias or dependence would call for reconsidering the model, but is not proven by one small batch.

recovery.question: When should the fair independent coin model be reconsidered, per the source?

choices.text: If the coin is biased or tosses are dependent.
Whenever four tosses do not give exactly two heads.
Never; the model is always correct.

recovery.explanation: cue-6 names bias or dependence as reasons to reconsider the model, while noting small batches need not match expectations.

glossary.definition: Knowing the result of one toss does not change the probability distribution for the next toss.
An elementary result of two tosses where order matters, e.g., HT and TH are distinct; each of the four has probability one quarter.
Finding the probability of an event by subtracting the probability of its opposite from one, e.g., P(at least one head) = 1 − P(TT).
